sentences.text: He anchored his last ships in a roaring strait, with an enemy fleet so close he could hear them laughing.
His captain grabs his collar.
"They've got ten ships for every one of ours, and you're parking?"
He doesn't look up.
He just drops a cork over the side and watches it drift.
"Wait for the water," he says.
"Watch the cork."
Then the enemy charges into the strait, the current carrying them in like a river.
Their admiral is thrilled.
The sea is doing all the rowing.
His own captains anchor well behind him, politely letting him face the enemy first.
But the strait is so narrow only a few ships fit at once, and his cannons keep those busy.
Meanwhile, the cork is slowing down.
Then it stops dead, just as the enemy flagship pulls close enough to spit on.
You see, some narrow straits really do this.
The tide runs through like a river, and every few hours it stops and turns around.
Now the water that rushed them in shoves them back, harder than they can row.
His ships are anchored.
Theirs aren't.
Their front ships pile into the ones behind, and his cannons pound the jam.
By sunset, the whole enemy fleet is drifting backwards out of the strait, their admiral close enough to wave goodbye.
His captain, who called it parking, now says it was his idea.
And the cork drifts right back past him, going the other way.
